title: Arrival Lattice Warmup + Thermal Flush Playbook
content:
Purpose and motivation:

This is a working playbook for a warmup and cooldown pattern we call an "arrival lattice" plus a "thermal flush". Goal: get repeatable throughput numbers that are resilient to microburst artifacts, GPU thermals, and client-side RNG noise without adding excessive wall-clock time. Use for: steady-state throughput claims, scaling sweeps, and modeling latency/throughput hysteresis.

Why this is different:
- Existing warmup recipes (staircase, priming anchors) help but often leave residual thermal or memory fragmentation effects that taint long runs.
- "Arrival lattice" mixes high-frequency microbursts and low-frequency steady arrivals so we exercise both scheduling and batching layers.
- "Thermal flush" is an explicit cooldown/flush step to reset thermal plateau and free transient allocations between trial runs.

High-level recipe (summary):
1) Pre-checks (5m): verify GPU clocks, free memory, node labels; abort on >5% clock drift.
2) Dry priming phase (3m): short calls with small batch-size to populate KV cache and load kernels.
3) Arrival lattice warmup (8-12m): alternating microburst lanes and steady lanes (see lattice config below).
4) Measurement window (10m+): fixed arrival pattern locked to the steady lane of the lattice to get throughput samples.
5) Thermal flush (3-5m): controlled idle + synthetic low-priority background to accelerate thermal decay and clear transient state.
6) Cool validation run (3m): quick smoke to ensure metrics returned to baseline.

Detailed steps and rationale:

Pre-checks (scripted, non-blocking):
- Query GPU clocks and temperatures: if temperature > 55C at start, tag run with "warm-slate" and optionally abort.
- Ensure no other user containers on node; swap disabled; cgroups checked.
- Pull model artifact and verify checksums.
- Record driver and CUDA/cuDNN versions in run metadata.

Dry priming phase (what & why):
- Duration: 3 minutes.
- Pattern: 50 qps of shortest inference (length 8 tokens, batch_size=1) with 20% random jitter.
- Purpose: populate kernel caches, warm memory allocator, warm up JITs, and ensure model weights are resident.
- Notes: Do not record metrics from this phase to final dataset; log separately.

Arrival lattice warmup (config):
- Concept: two interleaved lanes run concurrently from the client side:
  - Microburst lane (MB): short bursts of very high concurrency for short windows (e.g., 500ms bursts at 4x target QPS).
  - Steady lane (SL): continuous constant-rate traffic at target throughput.
- Typical params for a target steady throughput T (qps):
  - SL: Poisson/constant at T qps, jitter 5%
  - MB: bursts of duration 0.4-0.6s, spaced every 6-12s, burst peak 3-6x T, duty cycle 6-10%
  - Total warmup duration: 8-12m (scale up for larger clusters)
- Implementation hint: spawn N client workers, each configured to run both lanes with deterministic seed so runs are repeatable.

Why lattice helps:
- Microbursts expose batch formation latencies, GPU scheduling fairness, and queuing hysteresis without keeping the system in perpetual high-temp state.
- Interleaving ensures that batching logic cannot adapt only to steady inputs; it must also handle burst-fanouts.

Measurement window and sampling rules:
- Start measurement after the lattice warmup completes and immediately switch to the SL-only pattern (T qps constant).
- Measurement duration baseline: 10 minutes; increase to 30 minutes for large-capacity claims.
- Metrics to capture (sample every 5s): throughput qps, p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec from server, GPU util, GPU total power, kernel-launch rates, free memory, context-switch rates, and scheduler queue depth.
- Log sampling must be clock-synchronized; prefer server-side timestamps with NTP drift <1s.

Thermal flush (why & how):
- Problem: Consecutive runs on the same node tend to show slowly drifting throughput as GPU thermal governor ramps down clocks, and memory allocators fragment. Over many runs this biases comparisons.
- Thermal flush recipe:
  - Step 1: quiesce traffic for X seconds where X = min(60, 1.5 * average HLC decay window). Typically 90-180s on datacenter GPUs.
  - Step 2: run low-priority background kernel that toggles SM-level activity at 10-20% duty cycle for 60s to homogenize thermal plateaus (synthetic workload should be memory-light to avoid persistence).
  - Step 3: run GPU memory defrag utility (or restart allocator service) if available; otherwise, wait additional 30s idle.
- Tag runs with "thermal-flush-v1" so we can filter comparisons.

Run naming and metadata convention (important for traceability):
- run_id: <date>-<owner_initials>-<target_qps>-<seed>-<variant>
  e.g., 20250112-AK-250-321-v1
- metadata fields: model_name, quantization, batch_size, seq_len, hw_pool, driver, cuda, warmup_recipe, lattice_params, thermal_flush_used (true/false), notes.

Repeatability checklist (pre-run):
- [ ] Node labels pinned (gpu-type, zone).
- [ ] Single-run processes cleared; no other tenant jobs.
- [ ] RNG seeds supplied to loadgen and client worker threads.
- [ ] Baseline clocks within expected tolerance.
- [ ] Observability hooks enabled (prometheus scrape + perf counters).

Troubleshooting heuristics (notes to self):
- If p99 spikes correlate with MB bursts in measurement window: adjust microburst duty or increase measurement duration.
- If throughput drifts down over multiple sequential runs: confirm thermal-flush performed and check power-capping/policy.
- If measurements vary across runs with same seed: investigate non-determinism in request routing (multi-CPU scheduler) and client-side timer rounding.

Sample loadgen config (CLI/psuedo-json):
- clients: 64
- seed: 321
- sl_rate: 250  # qps per system (steady lane)
- mb_peak: 1250  # peak qps in microburst lane
- mb_dur_ms: 500
- mb_interval_s: 8
- jitter_pct: 5
- record_interval_s: 5

Quick pasteable client command (example):
python loadgen.py --clients 64 --seed 321 --steady 250 --burst-peak 1250 --burst-dur 0.5 --burst-interval 8 --duration 720  # seconds (12m)

Data analysis templates (what to look for):
- Throughput stability: coefficient of variation across sliding 60s windows should be < 2.5% for final claim.
- Latency tail coupling: p99 should not increase >15% when moving from steady-only to lattice-with-mb in the warmup. If it does, check batching timeouts.
- Thermal coupling: correlate GPU power curve with throughput; if throughput plateaus decrease while temp increases, this is thermal throttling.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Find lower-overhead method to do allocator-level defrag without restarting containers.
- Tune background synthetic kernel for different GPU generations (A100 vs H100 vs L40). Current numbers are empirical; need systematic sweep.
- Add built-in support to loadgen for lattice patterns to reduce per-experiment scripting drift. (See github issue linked above.)

Appendix: quick notes and experiment log template:
- experiment_20250113_AK_250_v1: observed 0.8% CV over 10m window; thermal-flush reduced run-to-run bias by ~1.6% vs no-flush.
- experiment_20250114_DM_500_v2: MB duty at 8% caused transient batching spikes; increased jitter to 8% smoothed p95.

References and links:
- perf issue: PERF-842 (see linked_artifacts)
- internal slack thread: #perf-bench-priming (search for "arrival lattice")

Notes to readers: this is a working doc. Please try the lattice on 1 node first and leave experiment logs under /shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/bench-journal/ with JSON metadata. If you update the recipe, add a short rationale and stamp the date.
